title: Why Anthropic's big IPO couldn't revive the AI trade
excerpt: Anthropic's IPO did nothing to dispel the headwinds facing the tech sector, which include higher borrowing costs and the specter of more regulation.

By William Edwards

Anthropic's IPO on Thursday couldn't get the bulls going again.

The Claude maker had a stellar first day of trading, opening at $111.50 a share, 34% above its IPO price of $83, ending the day up 17% after a historic offering that could be considered a success by most metrics.

Friday has been a different story. The stock is down 13%, trading barely above its IPO price and taking it on the chin with the rest of the market. The Nasdaq Composite turned red for the year and the S&P 500 fell into a correction.

So, why couldn't a hugely anticipated AI IPO revive the rally in tech?

The offering came at a down-and-out moment for AI stocks. Rising borrowing costs and a blue-wave election outcome have put the trade on a losing streak, as investors worry about a slowdown in the data center buildout. Investors had thus pinned their hopes on Anthropic.

On Thursday, Rebecca Walser, the chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, called the IPO "exactly what the market needs" to lift sentiment.

Dan Ives, the founder of Yorkville Ives and a perennial tech bull, issued a similar analysis in a client note on Thursday.

"At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic's debut is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives wrote.

That's not what's playing out a day after the IPO.

A big reason for that is structural, sources say. There's only so much capital to go around, and investors were dumping other assets to fund their purchases of Anthropic shares on Thursday.

"Anthropic is the new shiny object in the AI space, and for good reason: its product is virtually everywhere in the business community, and investors are taking notice," said Gaurav Mallik, chief investment officer at Modera Wealth Management. "Anthropic is at the heart of the AI rotation that is taking place, as investors opt to increase the diversification of their AI exposure so that it's not solely in semiconductors."

Throw in $2 trillion in market cap for Anthropic to soak up in an already weakening AI trade, and it may cause some problems.

Yet, while that explains Thursday's price action, the whole market, Anthropic included, was plummeting on on Friday.

The big declines point at a bigger problem than a brief rotation into a new stock: the Anthropic IPO does nothing to solve the woes that were already facing the AI trade, namely, rising borrowing costs, concerns about regulation, and the ability for hyperscalers to sufficiently monetize their huge investments in the technology.

Not to mention, the de facto leader of the AI trade, Jensen Huang — and all his dealmaking — are gone from Nvidia.

Huang had positioned the chipmaker as a the central bank of AI, and now that he's gone following a series of scandals, stricter underwriting of new financing could make it harder for the deals to continue, said David Rosenberg, founder of Rosenberg Research, in a client note on Friday.

Rosenberg added that Nvidia's troubles have in turn caused the value of each of its investments to decline, setting up the AI trade to tailspin.

Plus, there are macro factors at play. Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said on Friday that the prospect of hawkish Federal Reserve policy amid sticky inflation is one reason cold water is being thrown on the AI trade in recent days.

"The Federal Reserve has added another layer of pressure. Minutes from the October meeting reinforced expectations that further tightening will be necessary to contain inflation, with markets now pricing an almost certain 25-basis-point hike in December," Hathorn said in an email.

"However, the bigger uncertainty is how much further rates may need to rise in 2027," she continued. "Elevated borrowing costs are particularly challenging for technology companies, while persistent uncertainty around the terminal rate has contributed to volatility across Treasury markets."
